newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Britain to review utility regulation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Britain to review utility regulation.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government launched a major review of the regulation of utilities on Monday, aiming to establish a long-term stable framework for overseeing the privatised companies.

The review was welcomed by existing watchdogs and by consumer groups, and came as one water company announced it was returning more cash to shareholders. Shares in utilities showed little reaction to the news.

Trade and Industry Secretary Margaret Beckett told a utilities conference the review would cover water, gas, electricity and telecommunications, with deputy Prime Minister John Prescott additionally looking at transport.

The government, which swept to power in a landslide victory on May 1, has been fiercely critical of hefty shareholder payouts, huge profits and pay packets and poor service of utilities, which were privatised by previous Conservative administrations.
It has vowed to levy a one-off tax on their excess profits to fund a programme to cut youth unemployment in its first Budget on July 2.

"Such a review of utility regulation is long overdue...we will be looking for a better balance between the interests of consumers and shareholders," a statement from the National Consumer Council (NCC) said.
The inter-departmental review will aim to develop general principles of regulation, Beckett said.

She said the review would look at "whether the current system of price regulation delivers...the greatest benefits to consumers while maintaining proper incentives for innovation and investment and an adequate return to shareholders."

It will consider pricing formulas, but Beckett ruled out regulation on the basis of rate of return on assets, and will look at defining the limits within which regulators work and try to identify best practice.
"Our objective is to set a long term stable framework for utility regulation which is and is seen as fair by all the interests involved, particularly by consumers," Beckett said.

The review will consider alternative structures for regulators including panels, boards or non-executive advisers, but Beckett said she would need persuading that there should be a "super-regulator" to oversee all regulation.
"I have some reservations on the notion of one person being charged with such a task," she told reporters.
At present, each industry is regulated by an autonomous body -- such as Ofgas, Oftel and Ofwat -- which each set their own pricing formula and rule on other matters.
"We welcome another review...the broad framework seems to us acceptable," said a spokesman for water watchdog Ofwat, adding that it would be happy to contribute.
Electricity watchdog Offer and telecommunications regulator Oftel echoed that view.
Changes in approach by individual regulators have at times made for uncertainty in sahres markets.
Shares in utility companies showed little reaction to the review, as analysts said it had been largely expected and was taking time to consider aspects of potential change.
"We're not looking at any new policy for a long time...we're not going to see any radical changes to the institutional setup over night," said one stock market analyst who asked not to be identified.
The review should reach conclusions by the end of the year, possibly by autumn, Beckett said, and if any changes in current frameworks are proposed, a consultation paper would be published.

Beckett said the review will take account of previous reports, including those from the parliamentary Public Accounts and Trade and Industry Committees, which criticised the amounts of profits made, and the Hansard Society, which called for clarity in regulation.
She said the views of current regulators would be very important. ($ = 0.601 British Pounds)
